Base directory for this skill: /Users/myankelev/.claude/skills/wayfinder

A loose idea has arrived — too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** — questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute — one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting — it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic — engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride *inside* the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed — they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like — the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index — one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link) — <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship — essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children — the edge of the known.

The answer isn't part of the body — it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

## Ticket Types

Every ticket is either **HITL** — human in the loop, worked *with* a human who speaks for themselves — or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

- **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a `/research` **subagent**. Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.
- **Prototype** (HITL): Raise the fidelity of the discussion by making a cheap, rough, concrete artifact to react to — an outline, a rough take, a stub, or UI/logic code via the /prototype skill. Links the prototype as an asset. Use when "how should it look" or "how should it behave" is the key question.
- **Grilling** (HITL): Conversation via the /grilling and /domain-modeling skills, one question at a time. The default case.
- **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a *decision* can be made — nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that *does* rather than decides — and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the human a precise checklist (HITL). Resolved when the work is done; the answer records what was done and any resulting facts (credentials location, new URLs, row counts) later tickets depend on.

## Fog of war

The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination — everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now — _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp — even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope** — it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates — the frontier stops at the destination — so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination — mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution — **close it** (a closed ticket is unambiguously off the frontier) and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why it's out of scope, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked — a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session** — with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Run a `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` session to pin down what this map is finding its way to — the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** — the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session — you don't need a map. Stop and ask the user how they'd like to proceed.
3. **Create the map** (label `wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.
4. **Create the tickets you can specify now** as child issues of the map — then wire blocking edges in a **second pass** (issues need ids before they can reference each other). Wiring sorts them into the frontier and the blocked; everything you can't yet specify stays in the fog — the **Not yet specified** section.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a `/research` subagent to resolve it in parallel, capturing its findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer from the ticket.
6. Stop — charting is one session's work; it hand-resolves nothing.

### Work through the map

User invokes with a map (URL or number). A ticket is **optional** — without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map** — the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first frontier ticket in order. **Claim it**: assign it to yourself before any work.
3. Resolve it — **zoom as needed**: fetch the full body of any related or closed ticket on demand; invoke the skills the `## Notes` block names. If in doubt, use `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling`.
4. Record the resolution: post the answer as a **resolution comment**, **close** the issue, and **append a context pointer** to the map's Decisions-so-far.
5. Add newly-surfaced tickets (create-then-wire); graduate any fog the answer has made specifiable, clearing each graduated patch from **Not yet specified** so it lives only as its new ticket. If the answer reveals a ticket — this one or another — sits beyond the destination, **rule it out of scope** rather than resolving it on the route. If the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets.

The user may run unblocked tickets in parallel, so expect other sessions to be editing the tracker concurrently.

{"body":"## Destination

A complete **rewrite blueprint** for CipherBox v2 — a full internal re-architecture on fixed pillars — together with a **standalone as-built spec corpus** documenting the current system (flows and data structures, not implementation). Both live in this repo. The map is done when the corpus is complete, every design decision is closed, and blueprint docs exist per v2 component — nothing left to decide before building v2.

## Notes

**Domain**: privacy-first E2EE personal cloud storage on IPFS/IPNS. Source implementation: [FSM1/cipher-box](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box) (local checkout at `~/Code/random/cipher-box`).

**Fixed pillars** (settled during charting — not tickets):

- Zero-knowledge server + client-side E2EE. The server never sees plaintext or unencrypted keys.
- IPFS + IPNS as substrate, with client-side cryptographic verification of records.
- Web3Auth key derivation for login.
- TypeScript web app + Rust desktop (Tauri + FUSE) split.

**IPNS boundary** (settled during charting): the IPFS network is canonical for IPNS records. Clients verify records cryptographically. CipherBox-hosted infra (Kubo, delegated routing) may exist as dumb accelerators, but nothing breaks if it vanishes, and the API database never serves records. Today's publish-path relay exists chiefly to give the TEE republisher a source of records — so resolution architecture and record liveness are one coupled design space.

**Corpus shape**: one spec per part (package/crate/app, twins paired) plus one spec per cross-cutting flow. Template and TOC are fixed by the template ticket; specs merge to `main` via PR.

**Skills**: grilling tickets → `/grilling` + `/domain-modeling`; prototype tickets → `/prototype`; research tickets → `/research` subagents.

**Execution override**: producing the as-built specs and the final blueprint docs in this repo IS in scope for this map — deliverables, not just decisions.

**Tracker mechanics**: tickets are sub-issues of this map; blocking uses GitHub's native blocked-by relationships (frontier = open, unblocked, unassigned); claiming = assign yourself. AFK research agents post their resolution comment and close their ticket but do not edit this map body — the next session appends their entry to Decisions so far.

**gh quirk**: run `gh` as `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh …` in this environment.

- [Decide: v1 vault migration stance](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/6) — clean break on both axes: no data migration (re-upload plaintext; no migration ticket), no identity obligation (v2 auth free to keep or change Web3Auth config on merit; v1 is staging-only, all-DEVNET, MAINNET never used, production gated on funding).
- [Design: decentralized IPNS resolution and publish](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/23) — delegated-routing-first on both surfaces with mandatory client-side verify (@helia/ipns; Rust /routing/v1 client); someguy as pure accelerator, public endpoints as fallback; desktop kad backend defer designed-for behind a routing trait; API fully out of the publish plane (direct fan-out, ≥1 ack); optimistic CAS + rebase with IPNS sequence as the clock; cache-first UI, never block on resolve.
- [Design: record liveness and the republisher](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/24) — 90-day client-signed EOLs make liveness a keyless re-PUT job (online clients hourly + in-API republisher module ~12h from a pin-derived, server-auditable name inventory, non-canonical record cache + recovery endpoint); TEE dropped designed-for (no enclave/Phala/epochs in v2.0, re-signer seam documented); client-side lease renewal at seq+1 replaces TEE re-signing; retirement = inventory removal, replacing tombstones.
- [Design: sharing and grant delivery architecture](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/25) — grants-in-metadata: blinded-tag ECIES blobs in the envelope + write-body ledger + owner-signed grant-set commitment (replaces recipientPins, owner-only grant authority); relay reduced to until-acked sealed pointer mailbox + people directory; durable share lists in each party's own vault (revocation discovered, not delivered); read revoke = immediate cut (supersedes ADR 0002 lazy), write revoke = write rotation (ADR 0001 upheld); files first-class grant targets; invites = bearer links incl. write-capable → cheap write rotation becomes a hard rotation-ticket requirement.

- [Design: seal authentication and floor re-anchor for seed-bearing structures](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/39) — relay forgery closed by the now-normative record-verify chain (adversary = rogue write-grantee); committed writer pseudonyms (pairwise-ECDH-derived, commitment-listed) detached-sign every seed-bearing structure, enforced whole-record fail-closed as a new adoption-gate stage; floors advance only on AAD-confirmed unseals, cold-seeded from a new owner-vouched `minReadEpoch` in the re-point object; owner entry canonical from an own-vault seed cache (owner blob demoted to accelerator, ascent pubkeys derive-and-verified); vault pointer gains the signed re-point payload + an indexed key chain (never-rotates retired); F-8 duplicates fail-closed with name-in-AAD rejected, F-9 KDF edge catalog frozen, mailbox payloads sender-authenticated; schema pile +6.
- [Design: v2 component decomposition](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/28) — engines-in-one-Rust-core: crates/{core,engine,fuse,wasm} + packages/client + apps/{web,desktop,api}; core owns IPNS end-to-end via dumb /routing/v1 HTTP seams (supersedes the per-host library picks in [Design: decentralized IPNS resolution and publish](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/23) — @helia/ipns dropped); worker-hosted WASM engine with RPC facade + tab leadership; one hand-written Rust API client inside the engine (no generated clients, api-client packages die); server-owned OpenAPI artifact + live contract tests (sdk-e2e descendant); v2 rebuilds in the cipher-box repo on its existing CI/e2e infra, v1 frozen on a branch, release management redone.
- [Blueprint: core](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/43) — blueprint/core.md; strict-canonical decode with unknown-field round-trip, 14-edge frozen KDF catalog, Ed25519 writer pseudonyms, manifest-driven single-implementation KAT regime (accept+reject vectors, separation KAT, fixed-ephemeral HPKE KATs).
- [Blueprint: engine](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/44) — blueprint/engine.md; single stateful brain over nine dumb host-seam traits, six-stage adoption gate with pointer-driven floors, amended eager-set rotation + cross-scope-move re-seal, hand-written API client; CONTEXT.md eager-set/forgery-window glossary staleness fixed in [PR 51](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/pull/51).
- [Blueprint: web client](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/45) — blueprint/web-client.md; one engine per origin in the leader tab (Web Locks election, thin-mirror follower tabs, seam-rehydrated failover), no degraded floor tier (cold-seed covers wipes), routes on stable node ids, SW demoted to dumb streaming pipe + app-shell precache.
- [Blueprint: desktop](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/46) — blueprint/desktop.md; key-free FS projection over the natively linked engine, vfs-level host adapters with push invalidation (FUSE-T SMB now, FSKit designed-for successor), journal generalized into the engine op queue, never-block law.
- [Blueprint: testing and verification strategy](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/47) — blueprint/testing.md; engine simulation harness as the center of gravity, contract suite keeps sdk-e2e's PR-blocking slot, e2e smoke on PRs + revert-first main matrix, structural anti-vacuity over coverage ratchets, mock-ipns-routing promoted to the CI routing store; api.md contract-and-clients amendment.

- (none — the route is fully ticketed: [Blueprint: deployment, infra and release management](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/48) is the final ticket to the destination.)

## Out of scope

- Executing the v2 rewrite (building it). This map ends at the blueprint.
- v1 maintenance and bugfixes in cipher-box.

=== FSM1 ===
Input from [Design: v2 metadata schemas and crypto envelope](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/27): codec, seal/unseal, derivation, and record verification are one Rust core compiled to WASM for the web; TS has no codec or crypto of its own. Decomposition should treat that crate as the shared foundation of both apps.
=== FSM1 ===
## Resolution

### D1 — Core boundary: engines live in the single Rust core

The one-Rust-core decision from [Design: v2 metadata schemas and crypto envelope](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/27) extends upward through the engines. One Rust implementation of the rotation primitives, adoption gate + floors, op-rebase/sync core, grant management, pointer planes, and mailbox logic — desktop links it natively, web loads it as WASM. TS keeps no engine logic. This is what the mandated constructor seams ([Design: key rotation model](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/26)) and "one model, two trigger sources" ([Design: sync, refresh and offline model](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/33)) were pointing at; it kills the v1 twin-drift disease (13 ungated resolve sites, the 8-row acceptance-divergence table) at the layer where it was most dangerous.

### D2 — IPNS stack: core owns records end-to-end; transports are dumb byte movers

Supersedes the per-host library picks in [Design: decentralized IPNS resolution and publish](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/23): `@helia/ipns` is dropped, and no rust-ipns crate decision is needed beyond what the core hand-rolls. The core owns record create/sign/verify/marshal on both platforms (one implementation, one KAT set); the injected transport seam is a trivial `/routing/v1` HTTP client — `fetch` on web, `reqwest` on desktop — moving opaque record bytes only. Everything else in that ticket (delegated-routing-first, someguy as accelerator, fan-out publish, CAS + rebase) stands.

### D3 — Workspace layout

```text
crates/
  core/     wire formats, crypto, seal/unseal, KDF catalog,
            IPNS records, KATs — pure, deterministic
  engine/   rotation primitives, adoption gate + floors,
            op-rebase/sync core, grants, pointer planes,
            mailbox logic, API client — host seams as traits
  fuse/     FS core behind the host-adapter trait
  wasm/     wasm-bindgen bindings over core + engine

apps/
  desktop/  Tauri shell, links engine natively
  web/      React UI only — no crypto, no seams
  api/      NestJS residual surface + in-process republisher module

packages/
  client/   TS wrapper over WASM: typed API, browser seams
            (IndexedDB floors, fetch transports, OPFS staging),
            worker wiring, tab leadership
```

Split rationale: `core` is deterministic and KAT-pinned; `engine` is stateful with seam traits. Consequences: all five v1 TS packages (`crypto`, `core`, `sdk-core`, `sdk`, `api-client`) and `crates/{crypto,core,sdk,api-client}` die; `apps/tee-worker` is deleted per [Design: record liveness and the republisher](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/24).

### D4 — WASM hosting: worker-hosted engine

One long-lived engine instance in a dedicated worker; `packages/client` exposes an async RPC facade to the UI thread and owns tab coordination (leader election, one engine writer across tabs). Streaming-decrypt/service-worker detail is web-blueprint territory, not fixed here.

### D5 — API client: one, hand-written, in Rust, inside the engine

The engine originates nearly all API traffic (registry on the publish path, mailbox, recovery, upload), so a single hand-written Rust client lives with it, using the injected HTTP seam — shared by web and desktop through the core. Token lifecycle lives in it too; the web app never touches tokens. No generated clients anywhere.

### D6 — API contract: server-owned spec, enforced by live contract tests

The NestJS API keeps emitting its OpenAPI spec (near-free from decorators), committed as a review/docs artifact. Enforcement is a live contract-test suite — the Rust client exercised against a real API instance in CI, the v2 descendant of sdk-e2e. Drift fails a test run, not a grep. No codegen in the loop.

### D7 — Repo: v2 rebuilds in the cipher-box repo on its existing infra

v1 is frozen on a branch (staging remains deployable from its last tag — there is no production), and `main` hosts the v2 workspace. Workflows, docker stacks, e2e harnesses, and scripts stay live and in-history, edited in place for the new layout; repo settings, secrets, environments, and review-bot integration are reused as-is. Release management — an acknowledged weak spot — gets redone as part of v2. cipher-box-next remains the planning/spec archive and this map's home.

### Graduation

Closing this ticket graduates six blueprint-doc tickets from the fog (one doc each in `blueprint/`, shape precedent `blueprint/api.md`): core, engine, web client, desktop, testing/verification strategy, and deployment/infra/release management. The `blueprint/api.md` amendment (client strategy, contract enforcement) rides the testing ticket.

1	# API residual role — v2 blueprint
2	
3	Resolved by [Design: API residual role and surface](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/34).
4	Normative for the v2 build. Upstream inputs: the
5	[resolution/publish](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/23),
6	[record liveness](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/24),
7	[sharing](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/25),
8	[rotation](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/26), and
9	[schema/envelope](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/27) designs;
10	client and contract strategy amended by the
11	[component decomposition](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/28)
12	(D5/D6).
13	
14	## Doctrine
15	
16	The v2 API is a **bookkeeping and accelerator service**, not a data plane. It never
17	serves IPNS records on any resolve path, never sees plaintext or unencrypted keys,
18	and holds no state a client cannot rebuild from the network plus its own vault.
19	Everything it does falls into five roles: authentication, pin/name bookkeeping
20	(quota + republish inventory), hosted content pinning, record liveness backstop,
21	and an integrity-untrusted mailbox.
22	
23	What left the API relative to v1 — with the design that removed it:
24	
25	| Gone | Removed by |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| IPNS publish/resolve relay endpoints | #23 — clients fan out `/routing/v1` PUTs directly |
28	| Record serving from the DB | #23/#24 — record cache is non-canonical, no client resolve path |
29	| `/shares`, `share_invites` | #25 — grants live in metadata; discovery rides the mailbox |
30	| People directory | #34 — never built; contact codes are self-authenticating |
31	| All TEE endpoints, `tee_key_state`, connection-test | #24 — TEE dropped, designed-for re-signer seam only |
32	| Vault init/export endpoints, `vaults` table | #27 — bootstrap is the derived vault pointer; export is client-side |
33	| `pin_migrations` | BYO re-pin is a client-side sweep over its own pin set |
34	| Download streaming through the API process | #34 — reads go to the trustless gateway |
35	| Generated `api-client` packages and the `api:generate` codegen loop | #28 D5/D6 — one hand-written Rust client in the engine; contract enforced by live tests |
36	
37	## Identity and auth
38	
39	- Account = the Web3Auth-derived secp256k1 **identity key**; challenge-signature
40	  login; SIWE wallet login stays as a secondary auth method (feature-set decision #5).
41	- Short-lived access JWT + rotating refresh token (HTTP-only cookie on web,
42	  OS keychain on desktop). Staging-gated test-login endpoint for e2e.
43	- Tables: `users` (keyed by `publicKey`; carries quota-limit override and BYO flag),
44	  `auth_methods`, `refresh_tokens`.
45	
46	## Pin/name registry
47	
48	The one surface every publish flow traverses. It feeds **both** quota and the
49	republisher inventory; its invariant is the central v1 lesson (silent enrollment
50	decay) inverted into structure.
51	
52	- **Endpoints**: batch register `[{ipnsName, headCid?, contentCids[]}]` and batch
53	  retire `[ipnsName | cid]`. Ordinary writes send single-item batches; name waves
54	  and sweeps send bulk. v1's BYO-only `register-cid` folds into the same register
55	  call.
56	- **Register-first, fail-closed**: registration precedes the first publish of a
57	  name, and publish is blocked on it. A live-but-uninventoried name is
58	  structurally impossible; the worst failure is a registered-never-published
59	  orphan, which the republisher's resolve-failure alert surfaces for GC.
60	- **Per-account rows, union liveness**: inventory row = `(account, ipnsName)`,
61	  pin row = `(account, cid, size)`. Whoever publishes registers under their own
62	  account — the server is zero-knowledge about the grant graph and authorizes
63	  nothing across accounts. The republisher walks **distinct** names; a name
64	  leaves the inventory when its last row is retired; physical unpin fires at
65	  global refcount zero (v1's `guardedUnpin` survives).
66	- **Shared scopes**: a write-grantee's uploads register (and count) under the
67	  grantee's account until the owner's client syncs, sees the new children, and
68	  registers them too — rows then coexist. Self-healing, permissionless.
69	- **Quota**: per-account sum over that account's pin rows. Hosted rows are
70	  authoritative and gate uploads; BYO accounts' rows are **advisory** (quota
71	  always allows, `advisory: true` in the quota response). Limit = env default
72	  plus per-account override column; no billing (out of scope).
73	- **Accepted exposure**: the server sees each account's flat name/CID counts,
74	  sizes, and churn timing — never tree structure, kinds, or names' relationships.
75	
76	### Write-rotation name churn
77	
78	- New names enroll automatically: the wave's publishes traverse register-first.
79	- Content CID rows are untouched by rotation (same CIDs re-referenced; upserts
80	  are idempotent). Old + new metadata head CIDs transiently double-count —
81	  metadata-scale only, accepted.
82	- **Interior fast, root lingers**: interior old names are batch-retired at wave
83	  completion (a resumed wave enumerates them via the write-plane history link).
84	  The old **scope-root** name stays registered, serving the owner-signed
85	  `movedTo` forwarding record, until the migration window closes — window
86	  length and closure signal are owned by
87	  [rotation completeness (#38)](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38)
88	  — then retired. The API stays dumb: retire removes the caller's row; timing is
89	  client policy.
90	
91	## Content plane
92	
93	- **Provider layer, registration always** (BYO-IPFS is first-class, carried from
94	  v1): the client's pin-provider abstraction decides where bytes go — hosted
95	  (default), external (own Kubo/PSA/Pinata endpoint), or dual. Every mode's
96	  publish flow still traverses the registry above; only the byte path varies.
97	  `ByoIpfsConfig` stays sealed in vault settings; provider connection testing is
98	  client-side (the TEE tester is gone).
99	- **Ingress (hosted)**: authenticated upload endpoint, quota-gated, pins to
100	  CipherBox Kubo, registers pins in the same traversal. BYO/dual bytes bypass
101	  the API entirely.
102	- **Egress**: the API process serves no bytes. CipherBox runs a Kubo-backed
103	  **trustless gateway** (block/CAR responses, client-side CID verification)
104	  gated by a CipherBox auth token — an accelerator for members. Any public
105	  trustless gateway is the no-auth fallback; reads survive CipherBox infra loss.
106	  Media streaming uses ranged block/CAR fetches through the existing
107	  service-worker decryption layer.
108	
109	## Republisher module and recovery
110	
111	Per the liveness design (#24), restated here as API surface:
112	
113	- In-process, worker-shaped, cleanly extractable module. Walks distinct
114	  inventory names on a ~12 h cadence: resolve from the network, re-PUT the same
115	  bytes (keyless). Alert when a name goes >24 h without a successful re-PUT.
116	- Non-canonical record cache table — rebuildable from the network, consulted by
117	  no client resolve path; refuses sequence-regressing records as
118	  unrelied-upon depth.
119	- **Recovery endpoint**: authenticated, rate-limited fetch of cached (possibly
120	  expired) record bytes by name — the revival aid after a >EOL lapse; a
121	  key-holder extracts the last CID and mints a fresh record.
122	
123	## Mailbox
124	
125	Integrity-untrusted, swappable transport for one-shot sealed pointers
126	(share pointers, write-rotation root re-points, invite claims, courtesy
127	notifications). Nothing on it is load-bearing for safety: root migration has
128	the `movedTo` record (#38), revocation is discovered in metadata.
129	
130	- **Post**: any authenticated account → recipient identity pubkey; body is the
131	  HPKE-sealed blob (≤ ~8 KB), sender supplies an idempotency key. Posts to
132	  unknown recipient pubkeys are rejected — an accepted, rate-limited,
133	  exact-pubkey existence oracle.
134	- **Poll**: recipient-authenticated; returns `{id, receivedAt, blob}` — no
135	  sender metadata in the clear (the sealed payload is owner-signed inside).
136	  Clients poll on the sync design's 30 s cadence; no push in v2.0 (push-ready
137	  seam per #33).
138	- **Ack**: delete by id. Retention: until acked, bounded — per-recipient
139	  pending cap (reject-new when full) and a 90-day unacked TTL aligned with
140	  record EOLs. Rate limits per sender account and per recipient mailbox.
141	- **Accepted exposure**: transient `{sender, recipient, timestamp}` edges;
142	  never a durable graph, never key material.
143	
144	## Contact exchange — no directory
145	
146	There is **no people directory**. This supersedes the sharing design's
147	directory component (#25) and resolves crypto-review finding F-6 structurally:
148	
149	- A **contact code** (QR / URL / pasted string) carries the self-authenticating
150	  bundle `{identityPk, encSubkey, bindingSig}` (~130 bytes). The engine verifies
151	  the binding signature against the carried identity key at import,
152	  **fail-closed and mandatory**. Invite URLs carry the owner's bundle the same
153	  way.
154	- Identity keys therefore only ever arrive out-of-band — there is no in-band
155	  lookup for a directory substitution attack to poison. Optional
156	  fingerprint-comparison UX remains available client-side for channel-MITM
157	  paranoia, but no server component is involved.
158	
159	## Account lifecycle
160	
161	- Accounts are created implicitly at first login; there is no vault-init
162	  endpoint — the first publish of the pointer and root rides the normal
163	  register-first flow.
164	- **Deletion: immediate hard-delete.** One authenticated call, client-confirmed;
165	  cascade: retire all inventory/pin rows (refcounted physical unpin), purge
166	  mailbox rows, delete auth rows. Sole-registered names stop being republished
167	  and decay from the DHT (~48 h); co-registered shared content survives via
168	  other accounts' rows. Nothing lingers server-side; keys still derive from the
169	  login secret, so a BYO self-hoster loses nothing they pin themselves.
170	
171	## Contract and clients
172	
173	Decomposition outcomes (#28 D5/D6), restated here as API surface:
174	
175	- **The spec is server-owned.** The NestJS API keeps emitting its OpenAPI
176	  document from decorators, committed as a review/docs artifact. It is
177	  documentation, not a build input.
178	- **No generated clients, anywhere.** The sole first-party consumer is the
179	  engine's single hand-written Rust client (engine.md); v1's generated
180	  `api-client` packages, the `api:generate` loop, and the staged-client
181	  pre-commit check all die with it.
182	- **Enforcement is live, not lexical.** The contract is enforced by the live
183	  contract-test suite — the engine's client exercised against a real API
184	  instance in CI, the sdk-e2e descendant. Drift between server behavior and
185	  client expectation fails a test run, not a grep or a codegen diff. Suite
186	  shape and gating are owned by
187	  [`blueprint/testing.md`](testing.md).
188	
189	## Ops
190	
191	Health endpoint; Prometheus metrics; a **working** global throttler with
192	per-surface limits (v1's inert `@Throttle` decorators are a named defect —
193	rate limiting must be verified effective in e2e); staging test hooks
194	(test-login) gated by environment.
195	
196	## Data model (complete)
197	
198	`users`, `auth_methods`, `refresh_tokens`, `name_inventory (account, ipnsName)`,
199	`pinned_cids (account, cid, size, advisory)`, `mailbox_messages`,
200	`record_cache` (non-canonical). Nothing else. No crypto-bearing rows outlive
201	their consumer; revocation-adjacent state is hard-deleted, never soft-flagged.
202	
203	## Hosted infra outside the API process
204	
205	- **someguy** — self-hosted `/routing/v1` delegated routing accelerator
206	  (resolve + publish target; public endpoints are fallback).
207	- **Kubo** — pin store and the token-authed trustless gateway.
208	
209	Nothing breaks if either vanishes: resolution falls back to public endpoints,
210	reads to public gateways, and the republisher is a liveness optimization, not a
211	correctness dependency.
212	
213	## Open edges
214	
215	- `movedTo` migration-window length and closure signal (drives when the old
216	  scope-root name is retired) → [#38](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38).
217	- Module boundaries are fixed by
218	  [#28](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/28) D3 (NestJS residual
219	  surface + in-process, extractable republisher module); the gateway/someguy
220	  deployment shape →
221	  [deployment blueprint (#48)](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/48).

# Deployment, infra and release management — v2 blueprint

Resolved by [Blueprint: deployment, infra and release management](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/48).
Normative for the v2 build. Upstream inputs: the
[component decomposition](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/28)
(D7: v2 rebuilds in the cipher-box repo, v1 frozen on a branch, infra edited
in place), the CI tiers and open edges handed here by
[`blueprint/testing.md`](testing.md) (runner provisioning, staging deploy
gates, release-tag e2e gating, nightly scheduling), the hosted-infra and
gateway shape from [`blueprint/api.md`](api.md), the Tauri updater from
[`blueprint/desktop.md`](desktop.md), the PWA install surface from
[`blueprint/web-client.md`](web-client.md), and the clean-break migration
stance ([#6](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/6)).

## Doctrine

v1's release machinery is the acknowledged weak spot this doc exists to
retire: sixteen components versioned independently drove a four-workflow
web — `release-please.yml` + `pr-release-preview.yml` + `release-gate.yml` +
`cargo-lock-release-sync.yml` — whose correctness depended on a bot commit
(`chore(release): set release targets`) surviving on every PR branch, a
`release-as` pin discipline enforced by nobody, and a two-tier Cargo.lock
sync racing the merge queue. All of that complexity served exactly zero
consumers: no package or crate was ever published to a registry. Three laws
replace it:

1. **One version, one train.** The repo releases as a single product,
   `vX.Y.Z`. The only release artifacts are the three deployables — the web
   bundle, the API image, the desktop installers. Internal crates and
   packages are unpublished implementation detail and carry no versions of
   their own.
2. **The release path writes nothing to PR branches.** Version bumps derive
   from conventional commits on `main`, period. Any design that requires a
   bot commit on a contributor branch to release correctly is rejected as a
   defect class, not tuned.
3. **Staging deploys are boring and destructive-restorable.** Staging is the
   only deployed environment (there is no production; it stays funding-gated
   and parked). Everything hosted is an accelerator by design (api.md), and
   the clean break (#6) removes all data-continuity obligations — so a
   deploy may always be "fresh volumes, redeploy, done", and cutover is a
   redeploy, not a migration.

What dies relative to v1 — with what killed it:

| Gone | Killed by |
| --- | --- |
| Independent per-component versioning, 16-entry manifest, component tags (`@cipherbox/web-vX`, `cipherbox-fuse-vX`, …) | law 1 — one product version, tag `vX.Y.Z` |
| `pr-release-preview.yml` + `.github/scripts/pr-release-preview.js` + the load-bearing bot commit + the force-push footgun | law 2 |
| `release-as` pins and the self-comparing changelog loop | law 1 — nothing to pin; one version moves forward |
| `cargo-lock-release-sync.yml` and the post-merge lock-sync fallback PR | crates are version-frozen (below); releases never touch Cargo.lock |
| `release-gate.yml` + `ci-e2e.yml`'s `retrigger-release-gate` polling | the main gate (testing.md) — release readiness is "main is green", asserted once at staging-tag time |
| The `--latest=false` un-marking loop in `release-please.yml` and `desktop-staging-release.yml`'s `mark-latest` | one release stream — the release carrying desktop artifacts is the only release, so `/releases/latest` is correct by construction |
| `build-tee` image job, `tee-worker` service, Phala compose files and deploy flow, `redis` in every stack | #24 — TEE dropped, republisher in-process; nothing queues, throttling and scheduling are in-process |
| `check-api-client.sh` pre-commit gate, `api-spec` drift CI job | #28 D5/D6 — no generated clients; the contract suite is the gate, OpenAPI freshness is a hygiene diff (testing.md) |
| `vector-parity` job, `check-vector-parity.sh`, vector generator scripts | the KAT-manifest regime (core.md) |
| SC#6/SC#2 grep gates in `cargo-linux` | testing.md law 2 — simulation scenarios, not source greps |

## v1 freeze mechanics

The freeze is one commit boundary, executed in this order:

1. **Cut the freeze branch.** Branch `v1` from `main` at the last v1
   release state, tag that commit `v1-freeze` (annotated). The branch is an
   archive and an emergency-redeploy source, not a maintenance line — v1
   maintenance is out of scope for this map.
2. **Close the open release-please PR** (never merge it) and any open v1
   PRs that won't be rebuilt onto v2.
3. **Hand `main` to the v2 workspace.** The first v2 commits on `main`
   delete the four dead release workflows and `pr-release-preview.js`,
   replace `release-please-config.json` + `.release-please-manifest.json`
   with the single-component config below, and begin the layout demolition.
   Workflows, docker files, and scripts are edited in place, in history —
   never forked into `-v2` copies.
4. **Re-point branch protection.** Required checks on `main` track the v2
   PR-gate job names as each suite lands (testing.md law 1: a suite exists
   only if it blocks merges). Job names are the contract; renames update
   the ruleset in the same PR.

Staging redeployability during the build: `deploy-staging.yml` is
tag-triggered, and workflow runs execute the workflow file **at the tag** —
so every existing `staging-*` tag remains a self-contained, reproducible v1
deploy with no dependency on `main` or the freeze branch. An emergency v1
redeploy is "re-run the last staging deploy run" (or re-push its tag).
`tag-staging.yml` stops functioning for v1 by design the moment `main` is
v2 — v1 mints no further releases.

During the build, before the first v2 release exists, staging deploys of
work-in-progress v2 come from a `workflow_dispatch` of the edited
`deploy-staging.yml` against a `main` SHA (no tag required). The tag-gated
flow below takes over at `v2.0.0`.

All v1 tags (component tags, `staging-*`) remain forever — history is
immutable; the `staging-` prefix keeps them disjoint from v2's `v*` tags.

## Release management

### Versioning and release-please

release-please stays — in its boring, single-component mode:

- **One manifest entry**: `.` (root, release-type `node`), component
  `cipher-box`, `include-component-in-tag: false` → tags are plain
  `vX.Y.Z`, starting at `v2.0.0`. One release PR, one CHANGELOG at the
  root, the same changelog-sections config. The GitHub App token mechanism
  (`RELEASE_BOT_APP_ID` / `RELEASE_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY`) ports so release-PR
  pushes still trigger CI.
- **Version surfaces are exactly two files**: the root `package.json` (the
  manifest source) and `apps/desktop/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (via
  `extra-files` — the surface the Tauri updater and the About dialog read).
  The API and web read the product version at build time (build arg /
  `define`) from the root — no per-app `version` fields to bump.
- **Crates and packages are version-frozen at `0.0.0`.** They are never
  published, so their manifest versions are meaningless; freezing them
  means a release never edits `Cargo.toml` or `Cargo.lock` — the entire v1
  lock-sync apparatus (both tiers, plus the disabled cargo-workspace-plugin
  workaround) has nothing left to do. `workspace.package` centralizes the
  frozen value.
- **Conventional commits keep feeding the bump**: `pr-title.yml` ports
  as-is (squash merges make the PR title the commit), including the
  no-parens-in-subject rule — release-please still parses subjects, and
  the rule costs nothing.

### Desktop release artifacts

On each `v*` tag, `desktop-release.yml` (v1's `desktop-staging-release.yml`
edited: trigger becomes the product tag, `mark-latest` deleted) builds the
Tauri installers for macOS/Windows/Linux via `tauri-action`, minisign-signed
with the carried `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY(_PASSWORD)` secrets,
`includeUpdaterJson: true`, and attaches them to the GitHub Release
release-please created for that tag. The updater doctrine is desktop.md's:
Tauri updater over GitHub releases, minisign-verified; with one release
stream, `/releases/latest` resolves correctly with no un-marking
choreography.

## Staging pipeline

### Release-tag gating (the v1 shape, simplified)

`tag-staging.yml` ports with its chain intact — it was the part of v1
release management that worked:

1. `workflow_dispatch` → assert `main` HEAD carries a `v*` tag (one regex,
   replacing v1's three-pattern component zoo). Untagged HEAD fails with
   "wait for release-please".
2. Re-run the e2e gates at that SHA via the reusable workflows — web,
   desktop mounted, and (new) the cross-client suite. This is the
   release-tag e2e gating testing.md handed here: the main gate already ran
   revert-first at merge time; this re-run is the deploy-time assertion
   that HEAD is still green, on the exact bits being shipped.
3. `staging-approval` environment gate (manual approval) → mint
   `staging-YYYYMMDD-release-N` → call `deploy-staging.yml`.

### The staging stack

`docker/docker-compose.staging.yml` edited in place. Same single VPS
(2 vCPU / 8 GB — the CPU budget note survives: Kubo capped, someguy never
starved), same GHCR image flow, same scp-env + `compose pull` + migrations
+ `up -d` mechanics in `deploy-vps`:

| Service | v2 disposition |
| --- | --- |
| `api` | ports — new image contents (residual surface + in-process republisher, api.md) |
| `postgres` | ports |
| `ipfs` (Kubo) | ports — pin store + trustless gateway upstream |
| `someguy` | ports — the self-hosted `/routing/v1` accelerator (staging/production only; CI uses the promoted mock, testing.md) |
| `caddy` | ports — static web + reverse proxy + the gateway auth front (below) |
| `alloy` | ports — Grafana Cloud shipping unchanged |
| `redis` | dies — nothing queues; throttling is in-process (verified effective by the contract suite) |
| `tee-worker` | dies (#24) — with it the Phala compose files, the CVM update ritual, and the simulator |

**Gateway deployment shape** (the api.md handoff): the token-authed
trustless gateway is Caddy in front of Kubo's gateway port —
`forward_auth` to a lightweight API token-verification endpoint, then
proxy to Kubo for block/CAR responses. The API process serves no bytes;
Caddy enforces membership; Kubo serves. Token format and TTL are API
build-time detail. Public trustless gateways remain the no-auth fallback,
so this path can fail without breaking reads.

**Web hosting**: Caddy keeps serving the static bundle from
`/opt/cipherbox/web` — but the artifact deployed is the production build
the e2e suite tested (testing.md: the artifact that ships is the artifact
tested). **PWA install surface** (the web-client.md handoff): v2.0 ships a
valid manifest and the decided SW app-shell precache, but does **not**
advertise installability — no install-prompt UX. Browser-menu install
works for those who seek it; install promotion is a post-v2.0 decision.

**Observability**: alloy → Grafana Cloud and the dashboard-provisioning
job port; the dashboards themselves are rewritten during the build (TEE
panels die, republisher inventory-walk and re-PUT metrics arrive; the
Kubo-version metrics caveat re-checked on the Kubo bump). Faro RUM in the
web build carries over.

**Landing page**: `deploy-landing.yml` and the Render preview path are
outside the v2 blast radius and port untouched, except fixing the known
env-name mismatch (`secrets.DNSLINK_RECORD_ID` vs the
`CLOUDFLARE_DNSLINK_RECORD_ID` variable, and the missing `environment:`
binding).

### Cutover

One scheduled, announced, destructive redeploy: stop the v1 stack, remove
the `postgres` and `ipfs` volumes, deploy the v2 stack fresh. No data
migration, no dual-running (#6 — v1 is staging-only, all-DEVNET). Staging
URL and Web3Auth config decisions carry per #6 (free to keep or change on
merit). One accepted consequence, stated: existing v1 desktop installs
auto-update into v2 via `/releases/latest` and their local vaults become
orphans — consistent with the clean break; the v2 first-run treats them as
new devices.

## CI infrastructure

### Runners

GitHub-hosted only; no self-hosted runners in v2.0.

- **PR gate**: `ubuntu-latest` for everything except the Windows adapter
  check (`windows-latest`). The browser suite (Playwright/chromium) and the
  contract-suite stack (Postgres + Kubo + mock routing store as GH
  services) both fit ubuntu. The PR e2e smoke slice runs on ubuntu only.
- **Main gate**: the mounted-desktop matrix keeps v1's three runner
  provisions — `macos-latest` + FUSE-T, `windows-latest` + pinned WinFsp
  MSI, `ubuntu-latest` + libfuse3/Xvfb. **Cross-client e2e rides the same
  matrix runners**: each OS leg runs the built web artifact headless
  alongside the mounted desktop against one stack — no fourth runner
  class, and cross-client gets per-OS coverage for free.
- **Toolchain single-sourcing** (fixes a v1 defect): a root
  `rust-toolchain.toml` becomes the one Rust pin — every job's
  `rustup default stable` line is deleted so CI builds what the repo pins.
  Node pins once in root `package.json` (`engines` + the existing
  `packageManager`), and workflows read it via `node-version-file` instead
  of sixteen hard-coded `'22'` strings. Dockerfiles align to the same
  major (the tee-worker `node:20` straggler dies with the app).

### Caching and hygiene

The v1 strategy ports: `setup-node` pnpm cache keyed on the lockfile;
`actions/cache` on cargo registry/git/target keyed per-OS on `Cargo.lock`.
The WASM build (`crates/wasm`, wasm-pack/wasm-bindgen) joins the cargo
cache key-space; `cargo-llvm-cov` and other cargo-installed tools move to a
cached install instead of v1's cold `cargo install` per run. Codecov ports
demoted to informational (testing.md): the upload jobs and
`codecov-base.yml` stay, thresholds stop gating. `zizmor.yml` and the
SHA-pinned-actions convention port as-is and apply to every edited
workflow.

### Scheduled tier

One new `nightly.yml` (cron) owns the scheduled slots testing.md defined:

- **Long-horizon liveness**: the compressed-EOL profile run — lease
  renewal at seq+1, the republisher inventory walk, >24 h-no-re-PUT
  alerting — nightly against the CI stack.
- **Full-matrix flake surveillance**: the main-gate e2e matrix re-run on
  `main` HEAD nightly. With `retries: 0` as policy, this distinguishes
  "main broke" (revert) from "environment drifted" (fix the harness)
  before it blocks a release.

Dispatch-only (unscheduled): the load harness against local or staging
(`load-test.yml` ports with its BYO scenarios), and the real Web3Auth
Core Kit login job against staging with the test credentials — the honest
inherited limitation testing.md records; never a PR gate.

| v1 workflow | Disposition |
| --- | --- |
| `ci.yml` | **Restructured** — skeleton, dorny path filters, service-container pattern, failure-artifact uploads port; jobs become the testing.md PR gate (lint/typecheck, cargo workspace + KAT/WASM, browser suite, contract suite, Windows adapter, migration drift, e2e smoke). `api-spec`, `vector-parity`, and the grep gates die (table above) |

| `deploy-staging.yml` | **Edited** — `build-tee` and redis plumbing out, gateway `forward_auth` wiring and volume-wipe cutover support in; VPS mechanics unchanged |
| `desktop-staging-release.yml` | **Becomes `desktop-release.yml`** — triggers on `v*`, attaches to the release-please release, `mark-latest` dies |
| `deploy-landing.yml` | **Ports** — env-name mismatch fixed |
| `load-test.yml` | **Ports** — dispatch-only |
| `pr-title.yml`, `zizmor.yml`, `codecov-base.yml` | **Port as-is** |

Docker, scripts, hooks:

| --- | --- |

| --- | --- |
| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY(_PASSWORD)`, `IDENTITY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY`, `STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET`, `STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET`, `STAGING_SSH_KEY`, `STAGING_DB_PASSWORD`, `STAGING_JWT_SECRET`, `WEB3AUTH_TEST_EMAIL/OTP`, `VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `RELEASE_BOT_*`, `CODECOV_TOKEN`, Grafana/Faro/Cloudflare families, `PINATA_JWT` (BYO load scenarios) | **Keep** |

- **Cutover trigger** — the criteria for scheduling the destructive
  redeploy (v2 contract suite + smoke green on a VPS dry-run); build-time
  judgment, announced in advance.

### Doctrine — three laws

1. **One version, one train.** The repo releases as a single product `vX.Y.Z`; the only release artifacts are the three deployables (web bundle, API image, desktop installers). Internal crates/packages are unpublished and carry no versions.
2. **The release path writes nothing to PR branches.** v1's load-bearing `chore(release)` bot commit is retired as a defect class, not tuned.

### v1 freeze

Branch `v1` + annotated tag `v1-freeze` at the last v1 release state; close the open release-please PR; first v2 commits on `main` delete the four dead release workflows (`pr-release-preview`, `release-gate`, `cargo-lock-release-sync`, plus the preview script) and install the single-component release config; branch protection tracks v2 gate job names as suites land. Existing `staging-*` tags remain self-contained v1 redeploys (workflow runs execute at the tag). Pre-`v2.0.0` staging deploys of WIP v2 go via `workflow_dispatch` of the edited `deploy-staging.yml` at a `main` SHA.

### Release management redo

release-please stays, single-component: one manifest entry (root), tag `vX.Y.Z` from `v2.0.0`, `include-component-in-tag: false`, app-token mechanism kept. Version surfaces are exactly two files — root `package.json` and `tauri.conf.json` (extra-files). **Crates and packages version-freeze at `0.0.0`**, so releases never edit `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` — the entire two-tier lock-sync apparatus has nothing left to do. `desktop-release.yml` (edited from `desktop-staging-release.yml`) builds minisign-signed Tauri installers on each `v*` tag and attaches them to the release-please release; with one release stream, `/releases/latest` is correct by construction (both un-latest hacks die).

`tag-staging.yml` chain ports (it was the part that worked): dispatch → single `v*` assert → web + desktop + **cross-client** e2e re-run at the tag SHA → `staging-approval` → `staging-YYYYMMDD-release-N` → deploy. GitHub-hosted runners only; PR gate on ubuntu (+ Windows adapter check); the main-gate mounted matrix keeps the 3-OS provisioning and **cross-client e2e rides those same matrix runners** (per-OS coverage, no fourth runner class).         if: steps.release.outputs.releases_created == 'true'
        env:

        run: |
          echo "## Releases Created" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

          echo "$RELEASES_OUTPUT" | jq '{releases_created, paths_released}' >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

          # resolves to the desktop release (marked latest by desktop-release.yml).
          # In manifest mode, release-please outputs tag_name (root) and
          # {path}--tag_name (per-package), so we match all keys ending with tag_name.
          TAGS=$(echo "$RELEASES_OUTPUT" | jq -r '
            to_entries
            | map(select(.key | test("tag_name$")))
            | map(.value)
            | unique[]
          ')

          if [ -z "$TAGS" ]; then
            echo "No tag outputs found — nothing to clear."
            exit 0
          fi

          for TAG in $TAGS; do
            [ -z "$TAG" ] && continue
            echo "Clearing latest flag for release: $TAG"
            SUCCESS=false
            for attempt in 1 2 3; do
              if gh release edit "$TAG" --repo "${{ github.repository }}" --latest=false; then
                SUCCESS=true
                break

              sleep $((attempt * 5))

            if [ "$SUCCESS" != "true" ]; then
              echo "::error::Failed to clear latest flag for $TAG after 3 attempts"
              exit 1
            fi

      # Cargo.toml version but does NOT update the workspace Cargo.lock's
      # [[package]] version lines, leaving main stale-on-first-cargo after a
      # release. The native cargo-workspace plugin is deliberately NOT enabled
      # (open bug googleapis/release-please#2517 skips Cargo.lock and manifest
      # updates in monorepo mode). The PRIMARY sync runs pre-merge in
      # cargo-lock-release-sync.yml (on the release PR branch, which is not
      # protected) so the synced lock lands atomically with the merge. This step
      # is only a fallback for the rare race where the PR merges before that job

      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        if: steps.release.outputs.releases_created == 'true'
        with:

          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Update Cargo.lock for released crates
        id: cargo-lock-sync
        if: steps.release.outputs.releases_created == 'true'
        env:
          RELEASES_OUTPUT: ${{ toJSON(steps.release.outputs) }}
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          # Map release-please package paths to their cargo package names.
          # The 5 crates/* are release-type rust; apps/desktop is release-type
          # node but bumps src-tauri/Cargo.toml (cipherbox-desktop) via extra-files.
          declare -A PKG_BY_PATH=(
            ["crates/api-client"]="cipherbox-api-client"
            ["crates/core"]="cipherbox-core"
            ["crates/crypto"]="cipherbox-crypto"
            ["crates/fuse"]="cipherbox-fuse"
            ["crates/sdk"]="cipherbox-sdk"
            ["apps/desktop"]="cipherbox-desktop"
          )

          # In manifest mode release-please emits "<path>--version" keys
          # alongside the path-less root "version". Pull every "<path>--version"
          # entry and update the matching first-party crate to that exact version.
          UPDATED=0
          while IFS=$'\t' read -r KEY VER; do
            # KEY looks like "crates/core--version"; strip the suffix.
            PATH_KEY="${KEY%--version}"
            PKG="${PKG_BY_PATH[$PATH_KEY]:-}"
            if [ -z "$PKG" ]; then
              continue
            fi
            if [ -z "$VER" ] || [ "$VER" = "null" ]; then
              continue
            fi
            echo "Syncing Cargo.lock: $PKG -> $VER (released path: $PATH_KEY)"

            to_entries
            | map(select(.key | endswith("--version")))
            | .[]
            | "\(.key)\t\(.value)"

          # normally syncs Cargo.lock on the release PR branch, so the merged lock
          # is already in sync and this is a no-op. An empty diff is success.
          if git diff --quiet -- Cargo.lock; then
            echo "Cargo.lock already in sync — nothing to do."
            exit 0
          fi

          # A non-empty diff means the pre-merge sync raced the merge (the release
          # PR was merged before that job pushed). main is a protected branch — we
          # CANNOT push to it directly — so open a follow-up PR with the synced
          # lock instead of failing the release. Never push to main here.
          echo "::warning::Cargo.lock stale after release (pre-merge sync raced the merge) — opening a sync PR."

          # (same GITHUB_SHA) targets the same sync branch instead of spawning a
          # new one. Each step below is made idempotent so a re-run after a prior

          # an existing remote branch would be rejected and abort the step.
          if git ls-remote --exit-code --heads origin "$SYNC_BRANCH" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "Sync branch $SYNC_BRANCH already exists — a prior fallback run pushed it."
          else
            git switch -c "$SYNC_BRANCH"
            git add Cargo.lock
            git commit -m "chore(ci): sync Cargo.lock for released crates"
            git push origin "HEAD:${SYNC_BRANCH}"
          fi

          # Open the PR only if one isn't already open for this branch — gh pr
          # create exits non-zero when a PR already exists for the head branch.
          EXISTING_PR=$(gh pr list --repo "${{ github.repository }}" \
            --head "$SYNC_BRANCH" --state open --json number --jq '.[0].number // empty')
          if [ -z "$EXISTING_PR" ]; then
            gh pr create \
              --repo "${{ github.repository }}" \
              --base "${GITHUB_REF_NAME:-main}" \
              --head "$SYNC_BRANCH" \
              --title "chore(ci): sync Cargo.lock for released crates" \
              --body "Automated Cargo.lock sync for released crate versions. The release PR merged before the pre-merge \`cargo-lock-release-sync\` job pushed the synced lock, so main's committed Cargo.lock is briefly out of sync with the bumped Cargo.toml versions. Merging this restores lock/manifest parity."
          else
            echo "PR #$EXISTING_PR already open for $SYNC_BRANCH — skipping create."

Before a release PR can be merged, the `release-gate.yml` workflow verifies that E2E tests have passed on the current `main` HEAD:

### Triggering a staging deploy

Staging deploys are triggered manually via the `tag-staging.yml` workflow (workflow dispatch in GitHub Actions). The workflow:

5. Creates a tag of the form `staging-YYYYMMDD-release-N` (N is a per-day sequential counter) and pushes it
6. Calls `deploy-staging.yml` as a reusable workflow
